entries.9:51: As the time approached for Jesus to be taken up to heaven, he set his face firmly toward Jerusalem. He was determined to go where God's plan led, even knowing it meant suffering.
entries.9:52: Jesus sent messengers ahead to a Samaritan village to get things ready for him. He made practical preparations as he traveled.
entries.9:53: The villagers refused to welcome him because he was heading to Jerusalem, which Samaritans opposed. People can reject Jesus for their own reasons, and following him may mean facing rejection.
entries.9:54: James and John wanted to call down fire from heaven to destroy the village. It's easy to want revenge when we're insulted, but that isn't the spirit Jesus wants.
entries.9:55: Jesus turned and rebuked them for their vengeful attitude. He corrects his followers when they mistake harshness for devotion.
entries.9:56: Instead of punishing the village, they simply moved on to another town. Sometimes the right response to rejection is to keep going peacefully.
entries.9:57: A man volunteered to follow Jesus wherever he went. It sounds bold, but Jesus tests whether he's counted the cost.
entries.9:58: Jesus answers that he has no home or security to offer, unlike even wild animals. Following him may mean giving up comfort and stability.
entries.9:59: Jesus invited another man to follow, but the man asked to bury his father first. Good things, even family duties, can become excuses to delay following Jesus.
entries.9:60: Jesus says to let the spiritually dead handle burial matters and to go proclaim God's kingdom instead. Following Jesus calls for urgent priority over everything else.
entries.9:61: Another man offered to follow but wanted to say goodbye to his family first. It sounds reasonable, but Jesus saw a heart still holding back.
entries.9:62: Jesus compares it to a farmer plowing while looking backward, which ruins the row. Following him requires full commitment and not constantly looking back at what we left behind.
entries.10:1: Jesus chose seventy more followers and sent them out in pairs ahead of him to the towns he planned to visit. It shows he wants many people involved in spreading his message, not just a few leaders.
entries.10:2: Jesus says there are many people ready to hear God's message but not enough people to tell them. He tells his followers to pray that God will send more workers.
entries.10:3: Jesus warns his messengers that they will face danger and hostility, like defenseless lambs among wolves. Following him can be risky, so they should expect opposition.
entries.10:4: Jesus tells them to travel light and not get distracted by long greetings along the way. The mission is urgent, so they should depend on God and keep moving.
entries.10:5: When they enter a home, they should begin by wishing it peace. It sets a tone of goodwill and shows the message they bring is one of peace.
entries.10:6: If the household welcomes peace, that blessing stays with them; if not, it returns to the messenger. A kind offer is never wasted, even when rejected.
entries.10:7: They should stay in one home and accept the food and pay offered there. People who work deserve to be supported, and staying put avoids appearing greedy.
entries.10:8: In any town that welcomes them, they should accept whatever hospitality is given. Receiving help graciously is part of the work.
entries.10:9: They should heal the sick and tell people that God's kingdom has come near. Caring for people's needs and announcing God's rule go together.
entries.10:10: If a town refuses to welcome them, they should go out into its streets and speak plainly. Rejection should be met with a clear, public response, not quiet resentment.
entries.10:11: Shaking off the town's dust is a visible sign that the town rejected God's message. Even when people refuse it, God's kingdom is still near and they are accountable.
entries.10:12: Jesus says the judgment on that town will be worse than on Sodom, a city known for great wickedness. Rejecting the message when you have heard it clearly carries serious weight.
entries.10:13: Jesus pronounces woe on towns that saw his miracles but did not turn from their sins. Seeing great evidence and still not changing is a serious matter.
entries.10:14: Tyre and Sidon, cities that never saw such miracles, will fare better on judgment day. More light given means more responsibility.
entries.10:15: Capernaum was proud of its closeness to Jesus' ministry, but Jesus says it will be brought low. Being near to God's work does not help if you don't respond to it.
entries.10:16: How people treat Jesus' messengers is how they treat Jesus and God who sent him. Accepting or rejecting the message is really about accepting or rejecting God.
entries.10:17: The seventy returned full of joy because even evil spirits obeyed them in Jesus' name. They were excited to see real power at work through them.
entries.10:18: Jesus describes seeing Satan fall like lightning from heaven. It pictures the defeat of evil that was happening through their mission.
entries.10:19: Jesus gives his followers authority over snakes, scorpions, and all the enemy's power, and promises nothing will truly harm them. They can face spiritual danger with confidence.
entries.10:20: Jesus tells them not to celebrate their power over spirits but that their names are written in heaven. The greatest joy is belonging to God, not having impressive abilities.
entries.10:21: Jesus rejoices that God reveals truth to humble, childlike people rather than to the proud and learned. God's ways often surprise the wise and lift up the simple.
entries.10:22: Jesus says everything has been entrusted to him by the Father, and only they truly know each other. Knowing God comes through Jesus, who chooses to reveal him.
entries.10:23: Jesus tells his disciples privately how fortunate they are to see what they see. Being present for these events is a privilege many longed for.
entries.10:24: Many prophets and kings wanted to see and hear what the disciples witnessed but never did. The disciples are living in a moment of great privilege.
entries.10:25: A legal expert stood up to test Jesus, asking what he must do to gain eternal life. He was probing Jesus rather than sincerely seeking an answer.
entries.10:26: Jesus turns the question back on him, asking what God's law says. He invites the man to answer from what he already knows.
entries.10:27: The man answers that we should love God with our whole heart, soul, strength, and mind, and love our neighbor as ourselves. This sums up what God asks of us.
entries.10:28: Jesus tells him he answered correctly and that doing this brings life. Knowing the right answer is not enough; it must be lived out.
entries.10:29: Wanting to justify himself, the man asks who counts as his neighbor. He is looking for a limit to his responsibility.
entries.10:30: Jesus tells of a man traveling from Jerusalem to Jericho who was robbed, beaten, and left half dead. The story sets up a situation where someone desperately needs help.
entries.10:31: A priest came by, saw the injured man, and passed on the other side. Even a religious leader avoided getting involved.
entries.10:32: A Levite, another religious worker, also saw the man and passed by on the other side. Both expected helpers failed to help.
entries.10:33: A Samaritan, a man from a group disliked by Jews, came along, saw the injured man, and felt deep pity. The unlikely outsider is the one who cared.
entries.10:34: He bandaged the man's wounds with oil and wine, put him on his own animal, and brought him to an inn to care for him. He gave real, costly help.
entries.10:35: The next day he paid the innkeeper and promised to cover any extra costs. His kindness was generous and went beyond the minimum.
entries.10:36: Jesus asks which of the three proved to be a neighbor to the injured man. He makes the point that being a neighbor is about showing mercy, not about status.
entries.10:37: The expert admits it was the one who showed mercy, and Jesus tells him to go and do the same. We are called to act with mercy toward whoever needs it.
entries.10:38: On their journey Jesus came to a town where a woman named Martha welcomed him into her home. She opened her house to him and his group.
entries.10:39: Her sister Mary sat at Jesus' feet and listened to his teaching. She chose to focus on learning from him.
entries.10:40: Martha was overwhelmed with serving and complained that Mary had left her to do all the work, asking Jesus to tell Mary to help. It's easy to resent others when we feel overloaded and unappreciated.
entries.10:41: Jesus gently tells Martha that she is letting herself get worried and upset over too many tasks. It means we can wear ourselves out with busyness, and Jesus invites us to notice when our worry has grown out of proportion.
entries.10:42: Jesus says only a few things really matter, and Mary chose the one best thing by sitting and listening to him. It means time spent with Jesus is worth more than any task and is something no one can take from you.
entries.11:1: Jesus was praying, and when he finished, one of his followers asked him to teach them how to pray, just as John the Baptist had taught his followers. It shows that even people close to Jesus wanted help learning to pray, so it's fine to ask for that help too.
entries.11:2: Jesus gave them a simple model prayer: address God as Father, honor his name, and look forward to his kingdom coming. It teaches us to start prayer by focusing on God and his purposes rather than only on ourselves.
entries.11:3: This asks God to provide the bread we need each day. It reminds us to depend on God for ordinary daily needs and to ask him for them.
entries.11:4: This asks God to forgive our sins in the same measure that we forgive those who owe us, and to keep us from being overcome by temptation. It means our own willingness to forgive is tied to how we ask for forgiveness.
entries.11:5: Jesus tells a story about someone who goes to a friend at midnight to borrow three loaves of bread. It sets up a picture of bold, persistent asking.
entries.11:6: The reason for the request is that a traveling friend has arrived and the host has no food to serve him. It shows the need is real and urgent, not trivial.
entries.11:7: The friend inside answers that the door is locked and his children are in bed, so he can't get up. It pictures a reluctant response to a persistent request.
entries.11:8: Jesus says that even if friendship alone won't move the man, sheer persistence will, and he'll give whatever is needed. It encourages us to keep asking God rather than giving up.
entries.11:9: Jesus tells his followers to keep asking, keep seeking, and keep knocking, with the promise that these efforts will be answered. It's an invitation to persistent, confident prayer.
entries.11:10: Everyone who asks receives, the one who seeks finds, and the one who knocks has the door opened. It reinforces that persistence in prayer is met with a response from God.
entries.11:11: Jesus asks which father would hand his son a stone when he asks for bread, or a snake instead of a fish. It points out that even imperfect parents know how to give good things.
entries.11:12: He adds that no father would give a scorpion when his son asks for an egg. The point is that parents naturally give what is good and safe.
entries.11:13: If sinful people know how to give good gifts to their children, God will far more surely give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him. It assures us that God's best gift is available to those who ask.
entries.11:14: Jesus drove a demon out of a man who couldn't speak, and when it left, the man could talk, which amazed the crowd. It shows Jesus' power over evil and the real change it brings.
entries.11:15: Some in the crowd claimed Jesus cast out demons by the power of Beelzebul, the prince of demons. They explained away a good deed with a hostile accusation.
entries.11:16: Others tested Jesus by demanding a sign from heaven. They wanted proof on their own terms rather than accepting what they had already seen.
entries.11:17: Knowing their thoughts, Jesus said any kingdom or household divided against itself falls apart. His point is that internal conflict destroys rather than builds.
entries.11:18: If Satan were fighting against himself, his kingdom couldn't stand, so their accusation makes no sense. Jesus shows the charge against him is self-contradictory.
entries.11:19: Jesus asks by whose power their own people cast out demons, and says those people will judge them. He turns their argument back on them.
entries.11:20: But if Jesus drives out demons by the finger of God, then God's kingdom has already come near to them. It means God's rule is arriving in real, visible ways.
entries.11:21: A strong man fully armed guards his house, and his possessions are safe. It pictures evil holding people securely under its power.
entries.11:22: But when someone stronger attacks and defeats him, he takes away the weapons the man trusted and divides his goods. Jesus is describing himself as the stronger one who overcomes evil.
entries.11:23: Whoever is not with Jesus is against him, and whoever doesn't help gather people to him scatters them. It means there's no neutral middle ground when it comes to Jesus.
entries.11:24: An evil spirit that leaves a person wanders through dry places looking for rest, and finding none, decides to return to the house it left. It pictures evil not simply disappearing but looking for a way back.
entries.11:25: When the spirit returns, it finds the house swept clean and put in order. The person's life looks tidy, but nothing has filled the empty space.
entries.11:26: The spirit brings seven worse spirits, and they move in, making the person's final state worse than before. It warns that cleaning up your life without filling it with God leaves room for worse trouble.
entries.11:27: A woman in the crowd called out that the mother who gave birth to and nursed Jesus must be happy. She was praising Jesus and his mother.
entries.11:28: Jesus replied that even happier are those who hear God's word and obey it. He shifts the focus from family connection to listening to and living out God's word.
entries.11:29: As the crowds grew, Jesus called that generation evil for demanding a sign, saying the only sign they'd get was the sign of Jonah. It means demands for proof can miss what God is already doing.
entries.11:30: Just as Jonah was a sign to the people of Nineveh, so Jesus would be a sign to his generation. His own life and message would be the evidence they needed.
entries.11:31: The queen of the South traveled far to hear Solomon's wisdom, and she will condemn this generation because something greater than Solomon is here. It warns against ignoring wisdom that is right in front of you.
entries.11:32: The people of Nineveh repented at Jonah's preaching, and they will condemn this generation because something greater than Jonah is here. It shows that greater evidence brings greater responsibility to respond.
entries.11:33: No one lights a lamp and hides it in a cellar or under a bowl; it's put on a stand so people can see the light. It means God's truth is meant to be seen and shared, not hidden.
entries.11:34: The eye is like a lamp for the body: a healthy eye fills you with light, but a bad eye leaves you in darkness. It's a picture of how what you focus on shapes your whole life.
entries.11:35: So be careful that the light you think you have isn't actually darkness. It's a warning to check whether what guides you is truly good.
entries.11:36: If your whole body is full of light with no dark part, it will be completely bright, like a lamp shining on you. It describes the wholeness that comes when nothing is left in darkness.
entries.11:37: While Jesus was speaking, a Pharisee invited him to eat, and Jesus went in and sat down. It shows Jesus was willing to share a meal even with those who would question him.
entries.11:38: The Pharisee was surprised that Jesus didn't wash before the meal. It reflects their concern with ritual purity customs.
entries.11:39: Jesus told him that Pharisees clean the outside of the cup and dish but are full of greed and wickedness inside. It means outward tidiness can hide an unclean heart.
entries.11:40: Jesus calls them foolish, asking whether the one who made the outside didn't also make the inside. It means God cares about both the outside and the inside, not just appearances.
entries.11:41: Jesus says that if you share what you have with poor people, that shows your heart is right and makes you clean on the inside. What matters to God is generosity, not just washing the outside.
entries.11:42: Jesus warns the Pharisees that they carefully give a tenth of even tiny garden herbs but ignore the far more important matters of justice and loving God. He tells them they should do the small things without neglecting the big ones.
entries.11:43: Jesus points out that the Pharisees love being noticed and respected in public. Wanting praise and the best seats for yourself is a warning sign of a wrong heart.
entries.11:44: Jesus compares the Pharisees to hidden graves that people walk over without realizing it, making them unclean. They look fine on the outside but quietly spread wrong influence on others.
entries.11:45: One of the experts in the law speaks up and tells Jesus that his harsh words insult them too. He is pushing back because Jesus' criticism hits close to home.
entries.11:46: Jesus answers that the experts in the law load people down with heavy rules but do nothing to help them carry the burden. It is wrong to demand of others what you are unwilling to do yourself.
entries.11:47: Jesus accuses them of building memorials to the prophets while their ancestors were the ones who killed those prophets. Honoring the dead does not make up for sharing the guilt of those who harmed them.
entries.11:48: Jesus says that by building these tombs they show they approve of what their ancestors did. You can share in someone's wrong by agreeing with it, even if you did not do it yourself.
entries.11:49: God in his wisdom said he would keep sending prophets and teachers to his people, and some of them would be killed and mistreated. God keeps reaching out even when people reject his messengers.
entries.11:50: Jesus says that the people of his own day will be held responsible for all the prophets' blood shed from the beginning. Guilt builds up when people keep rejecting God's messengers generation after generation.
entries.11:51: Jesus names the first and last murders of the prophets in the Bible, from Abel to Zechariah, and says this generation will answer for it all. God does not forget the wrong done to his messengers.
entries.11:52: Jesus says the experts in the law have taken away the key of knowledge, shutting people out of understanding God. They neither enter the truth themselves nor let others in.
entries.11:53: After Jesus left, the scribes and Pharisees pressed him hard with many angry questions. People who resist the truth often try to overwhelm it with arguments.
entries.11:54: They were watching Jesus closely, hoping to catch him saying something they could use against him. Not everyone who listens to you wants to learn; some are only looking for a reason to accuse.
entries.12:1: Jesus warned his followers that the Pharisees' hypocrisy was like yeast that spreads through dough. Watch out for people whose teaching looks good but is fake, because it can quietly infect your thinking.
entries.12:2: Nothing hidden stays hidden forever; every secret will eventually be exposed. Live honestly, because the truth about what you do will come out in the end.
entries.12:3: Whatever you say in private will one day be heard in public. Speak as if everyone could hear you, because secrets have a way of becoming known.
entries.12:4: Don't be afraid of people who can only kill your body; they can't do anything worse than that. Fear of people shouldn't control you.
entries.12:5: The one you should truly fear is God, who has authority over your soul beyond death. Take God seriously more than you take any human threat.
entries.12:6: Sparrows were sold cheaply, two for a penny, yet God remembers every single one. If God cares about birds worth almost nothing, he certainly cares about you.
entries.12:7: God knows even how many hairs are on your head. You matter far more to him than a whole flock of sparrows, so you don't need to be afraid.
entries.12:8: If you openly acknowledge Jesus before others, he will acknowledge you before God's angels. Standing with him publicly matters, and he will stand with you.
entries.12:9: If you deny knowing Jesus in front of others, he will deny knowing you before God's angels. What you say about him now has real consequences later.
entries.12:10: Speaking against Jesus can be forgiven, but speaking evil against the Holy Spirit cannot. This is a serious warning about rejecting God's own Spirit at work.
entries.12:11: When you're dragged before religious leaders or officials, don't panic about what to say. You don't have to prepare a defense in advance.
entries.12:12: The Holy Spirit will give you the right words at the exact moment you need them. You can trust God to speak through you under pressure.
entries.12:13: A man in the crowd asked Jesus to settle an inheritance dispute with his brother. He wanted Jesus to act as a judge in a family money fight.
entries.12:14: Jesus refused to be a judge or referee in that dispute. He made clear his mission wasn't about settling property arguments.
entries.12:15: Jesus warned the crowd to guard against greed of every kind. Your life isn't measured by how much stuff you own.
entries.12:16: Jesus told a story about a rich man whose land produced a huge harvest. The story shows what happens when abundance becomes the whole point of life.
entries.12:17: The rich man wondered what to do because he had nowhere to store all his crops. His problem was too much, not too little.
entries.12:18: He decided to tear down his barns and build bigger ones to hold everything. He put all his plans into storing up more for himself.
entries.12:19: He told himself to relax, eat, drink, and enjoy life because he had enough for years. He assumed his wealth guaranteed a secure future.
entries.12:20: God told him he was a fool: that very night he would die, and then who would get all his stuff? Death can end our plans in an instant.
entries.12:21: This is how it ends for anyone who piles up wealth for themselves but isn't rich toward God. Being rich in God's eyes is what actually counts.
entries.12:22: Jesus told his disciples not to worry about food or clothing. He wasn't saying these don't matter, but that worry shouldn't run your life.
entries.12:23: Life is worth more than food, and the body more than clothes. Don't let the things that keep you alive become bigger than life itself.
entries.12:24: Look at the ravens: they don't plant or store food, yet God feeds them. You are worth far more to God than birds, so trust him to provide.
entries.12:25: None of you can add even a little to your height by worrying. Worry simply doesn't accomplish what you hope it will.
entries.12:26: If you can't do even this small thing by worrying, why worry about everything else? Worry is powerless, so it makes no sense to give it your energy.
entries.12:27: Look at the wild flowers: they don't work or make clothes, yet they're more beautifully dressed than King Solomon in all his glory. God's care shows up in ordinary things.
entries.12:28: If God clothes grass that's here today and burned tomorrow, he'll surely clothe you. Don't let small faith keep you from trusting his care.
entries.12:29: Don't chase after food and drink or let your mind fill with doubt. Keep your focus steady instead of being consumed by what you'll eat and wear.
entries.12:30: People who don't know God run after all these things, but your Father already knows what you need. You don't have to scramble like those without a Father.
entries.12:31: Make God's kingdom your top priority, and everything else you need will be given to you as well. Put first things first and trust God for the rest.
entries.12:32: Don't be afraid, little flock, because your Father is glad to give you the kingdom. God isn't reluctant to bless you; he wants to.
entries.12:33: Sell what you have and give to the poor, and you'll build treasure that never wears out or gets stolen. Invest in what lasts forever instead of what rusts away.
entries.12:34: Your heart will follow wherever your treasure is. What you value most will shape what you care about and how you live.
entries.12:35: Be dressed and ready for action, with your lamps lit. Live alert and prepared, not caught off guard.
entries.12:36: Be like servants waiting for their master to return from a wedding, ready to open the door the moment he knocks. Stay ready for Jesus to come back.
entries.12:37: Those servants who are watching when the master returns are blessed, because he'll serve them at his own table. Jesus honors those who stay faithful and ready.
entries.12:38: Whether the master comes late in the night or even later, those servants who are watching are blessed. Faithfulness matters more than knowing the exact timing.
entries.12:39: A homeowner who knew when a thief was coming would stay awake and protect the house. Since you don't know the timing, stay alert.
entries.12:40: Be ready at all times, because Jesus will come when you least expect him. Readiness isn't optional; it's the whole point.
entries.12:41: Peter asks whether this warning about being ready is meant just for the disciples or for everyone. It invites each reader to hear these words as meant for them too.
entries.12:42: Jesus answers with a picture of a trusted manager left in charge of feeding the household. It asks who is faithfully doing the work they were given.
entries.12:43: The servant is blessed if his master finds him doing his job when he returns. It means being faithful in ordinary duties is what counts.
entries.12:44: The faithful servant is rewarded with greater responsibility over everything the master owns. Doing well with small trust leads to more.
entries.12:45: The bad servant assumes the master is delayed and starts bullying others and partying. It warns that delay can tempt us to live carelessly.
entries.12:46: The master returns unexpectedly and punishes that servant severely. It means no one can count on getting away with wrongdoing because the return comes unannounced.
entries.12:47: A servant who knew what was wanted but didn't prepare or obey gets a heavy punishment. Knowing what is right makes us more accountable.
entries.12:48: A servant who didn't know still gets a lighter punishment, and much is expected from those given much. The more you've been given, the more you're responsible for.
entries.12:49: Jesus says he came to bring fire to the earth and wishes it were already burning. It speaks of the serious division and judgment his coming brings.
entries.12:50: Jesus speaks of a baptism he must go through and feels pressure until it's finished. It points to the suffering and death he must face.
entries.12:51: People might expect Jesus to bring peace, but he says he brings division. Following him can split people apart, even those close to us.
entries.12:52: A household of five will be divided, three against two. It means loyalty to Jesus can divide even families.
entries.12:53: Family members will turn against each other because of him. It warns that faith in Jesus may cost close relationships.
entries.12:54: People can read a cloud in the west and predict rain. It shows we are good at reading ordinary signs.
entries.12:55: A south wind means heat, and people know it. It's another example of how well we read the weather.
entries.12:56: Jesus calls them hypocrites for reading the sky but missing what God is doing right now. It challenges us to notice what God is doing in our time.
entries.12:57: He asks why they can't judge for themselves what is right. It means we should think for ourselves about right and wrong instead of only following the crowd.
entries.12:58: If someone is taking you to court, settle with them on the way. It's practical wisdom to make peace before things get worse.
entries.12:59: If you don't settle, you'll stay in prison until the last penny is paid. It means unresolved debt or conflict has real consequences, so deal with it now.
entries.13:1: People told Jesus about some Galileans whom Pilate had killed while they were offering sacrifices, so their blood mixed with the blood of their offerings. It shows how shocking and violent the news was that people brought to Jesus.
entries.13:2: Jesus asked whether those Galileans suffered because they were worse sinners than other Galileans. He is challenging the common idea that bad things only happen to bad people.
entries.13:3: Jesus says no, they were not worse; but unless people turn their hearts around, they too will face ruin. The point is that everyone needs to change, not just judge others.
entries.13:4: Jesus brings up eighteen people killed when a tower at Siloam fell on them, and asks if they were worse sinners than everyone else in Jerusalem. Again he questions the assumption that tragedy proves someone was especially wicked.
entries.13:5: Jesus says no, they were not worse; but unless people change their hearts, they will meet the same kind of end. Everyone is called to turn to God, not to feel safe by comparing themselves to others.
entries.13:6: Jesus told a story about a man who had a fig tree in his garden and came looking for fruit but found none. It pictures God looking for real results in people's lives.
entries.13:7: The owner told the gardener that for three years he had found no fruit and wanted the tree cut down because it was wasting space. It shows that patience has a purpose and fruit is expected.
entries.13:8: The gardener asked for one more year, promising to dig around the tree and fertilize it. It shows God's patience and extra care, giving people more time to change.
entries.13:9: If the tree bears fruit after that, good; if not, it can be cut down. The point is that God's patience is meant to lead to real change, not to be taken for granted.
entries.13:10: Jesus was teaching in a synagogue on the Sabbath day. This sets the scene for what happens next.
entries.13:11: A woman there had been sick for eighteen years and was bent over, unable to straighten herself. Her long suffering shows how serious her need was.
entries.13:12: When Jesus saw her, he told her she was freed from her sickness. He took the initiative to help her without her even asking.
entries.13:13: Jesus put his hands on her, and she immediately stood up straight and praised God. Her healing led her to thank and honor God.
entries.13:14: The synagogue leader was angry that Jesus healed on the Sabbath and told the crowd to come on the other six days for healing. He cared more about his rule than about the woman being helped.
entries.13:15: Jesus answered that these men were pretending to be righteous, since each of them untied his ox or donkey and led it to water on the Sabbath. He pointed out their inconsistency.
entries.13:16: Jesus said this woman, a descendant of Abraham, had been bound by Satan for eighteen years, so it was right to free her on the Sabbath. He showed that doing good is always appropriate.
entries.13:17: When Jesus said this, his opponents were put to shame, and the whole crowd rejoiced over the wonderful things he did. The people recognized God's goodness at work.
entries.13:18: Jesus asked what God's kingdom is like and what comparison he could use. He is about to explain it with everyday pictures.
entries.13:19: He compared God's kingdom to a mustard seed a man planted in his garden, which grew into a tree where birds nested. Something small and ordinary grows into something large and welcoming.
entries.13:20: Jesus asked again what God's kingdom is like. He gives a second picture to help people understand it.
entries.13:21: He compared it to yeast a woman mixed into a large amount of flour until the whole batch was raised. God's kingdom works quietly but spreads through everything.
entries.13:22: Jesus continued traveling through towns and villages, teaching as he made his way toward Jerusalem. His journey was focused on his mission.
entries.13:23: Someone asked Jesus whether only a few people would be saved. Jesus answered by turning the question into a call for personal action.
entries.13:24: Jesus told them to make every effort to enter through the narrow door, because many will try but will not be able. It means salvation requires serious commitment, not casual interest.
entries.13:25: He pictured a house owner getting up and shutting the door, with people outside knocking and saying they know him, but he answers that he does not know where they come from. A time comes when it is too late to enter.
entries.13:26: Those outside will protest that they ate and drank with him and that he taught in their streets. They rely on being near him rather than truly knowing him.
entries.13:27: But he will say he does not know them or where they come from, and tell them to go away as people who do evil. Being familiar with Jesus is not the same as belonging to him.
entries.13:28: There will be crying and grief when they see Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the prophets in God's kingdom while they themselves are shut out. It shows the sadness of being excluded from God's family.
entries.13:29: People will come from east, west, north, and south and take their places in God's kingdom. God's kingdom is open to people from everywhere.
entries.13:30: Jesus said the last will be first and the first will be last. God does not rank people the way we do, and those we expect to be first may not be.
entries.13:31: Some Pharisees came and warned Jesus to leave because Herod wanted to kill him. It shows the danger Jesus faced as he continued his work.
entries.13:32: Jesus told them to tell that fox that he would keep driving out evil spirits and healing people today and tomorrow, and on the third day he would finish his work. He would not be scared off from doing God's will.
entries.13:33: Jesus said he had to keep going today, tomorrow, and the next day, because a prophet should not die outside Jerusalem. He was determined to complete his mission, even knowing the danger.
entries.13:34: Jesus expressed deep sorrow over Jerusalem, which killed the prophets and rejected those sent to her, longing to gather her people like a bird gathers its young, but they refused. It shows God's tender love and the pain of rejection.
entries.13:35: Jesus said Jerusalem's house would be left empty and they would not see him again until they welcomed the one who comes in the Lord's name. It warns of judgment while leaving hope for a future welcome.
entries.14:1: Jesus was invited to a meal at the home of a leading religious leader on the Sabbath, and the people there were closely watching him, hoping to catch him doing something wrong. It reminds us that people may watch how we live, so we should act with integrity.
entries.14:2: A man with a serious illness or swelling was right there in front of Jesus. His presence sets up the question of whether Jesus would help him even on a day when work was restricted.
entries.14:3: Jesus asked the religious experts and leaders a direct question: is it lawful to heal someone on the Sabbath, or not? He put the issue to them plainly so they would have to think about what really matters to God.
entries.14:4: They stayed silent, so Jesus healed the man and sent him on his way. Jesus did what was good and merciful even when others refused to speak up or approve.
entries.14:5: Jesus pointed out that any of them would pull their own ox or donkey out of a pit on the Sabbath without hesitation. If they would rescue an animal, surely a person in need deserves help too.
entries.14:6: They could not answer him, because his point was too obvious to argue with. Sometimes the right thing to do is clear, even when it makes people uncomfortable.
entries.14:7: Jesus noticed how the guests were grabbing the best seats for themselves, so he told them a story to teach them about humility. He used an everyday situation to show them something about their hearts.
entries.14:8: If you are invited to a banquet, don't rush to take the best seat, because someone more important than you might have been invited too. It's wise not to assume you are the most important person in the room.
entries.14:9: The host might ask you to move so the more important guest can have your seat, and you would be embarrassed as you take the lowest place. Assuming too much about your own importance can lead to humiliation.
entries.14:10: Instead, take the lowest seat, so the host can invite you to move up higher, and you will be honored in front of everyone. Humility is the safer and better path.
entries.14:11: Anyone who promotes himself will be brought down, but the person who humbles himself will be raised up. God values humility and resists pride, so we should not chase status.
entries.14:12: Jesus told the host not to invite only friends, family, and rich neighbors, because they can repay him with an invitation back. Giving only to those who can return the favor is not really generosity.
entries.14:13: Instead, invite the poor, the disabled, and those who cannot repay you when you give a feast. True generosity reaches out to people who have nothing to give back.
entries.14:14: You will be blessed because they cannot pay you back, and God will reward you at the resurrection of the righteous. God sees and rewards kindness shown to those who cannot return it.
entries.14:15: One of the guests said that anyone who gets to eat in God's kingdom is truly blessed. He was expressing admiration for the kingdom Jesus was talking about.
entries.14:16: Jesus responded with a story about a man who prepared a large banquet and invited many people. The story is about God inviting people to share in his kingdom.
entries.14:17: When everything was ready, the host sent his servant to tell the invited guests to come. The invitation was clear and the time had arrived.
entries.14:18: But they all began making excuses; the first said he had to go look at a field he had just bought. Ordinary concerns were used as reasons to turn down the invitation.
entries.14:19: Another said he had to go test some newly purchased cattle, so he could not come. Again, a practical matter was used as an excuse to refuse.
entries.14:20: A third said he had just gotten married and therefore could not come. Each excuse sounded reasonable, but all of them kept people away from the feast.
entries.14:21: The servant reported back, and the host became angry and told him to go quickly into the streets and bring in the poor, the disabled, and the blind. When the invited guests refused, the invitation was extended to those who had nothing.
entries.14:22: The servant said he had done what was ordered, but there was still room. There was more space to fill, showing that God's invitation is open to more people.
entries.14:23: The master told the servant to go out to the roads and fields and urge people to come in so his house would be full. God wants his house filled, and he actively reaches out to bring people in.
entries.14:24: Jesus concluded that none of those originally invited would taste his feast. Refusing God's invitation has real consequences.
entries.14:25: Large crowds were traveling with Jesus. He turned to address them directly about what following him really requires.
entries.14:26: Jesus said that anyone who comes to him must be willing to put him before even their closest family members and their own life. Following Jesus means he comes first, ahead of everything else.
entries.14:27: Anyone who does not carry his cross and follow Jesus cannot be his disciple. Following Jesus means accepting hardship and self-sacrifice, not just easy belief.
entries.14:28: If you wanted to build a tower, you would first sit down and figure out the cost to see if you had enough to finish it. Jesus wants people to think seriously about what following him will cost.
entries.14:29: Otherwise, if you start and cannot finish, everyone who sees it will laugh at you. Half-hearted commitment leads to failure and embarrassment.
entries.14:30: People would say, this person started building but couldn't finish. It's a warning to count the cost before you begin.
entries.14:31: A king going to war against another king would first consider whether his ten thousand men could defeat an army of twenty thousand. Wise people assess whether they are able to finish what they start.
entries.14:32: If he realizes he cannot win, he sends a delegation to ask for peace while the other king is still far away. It's better to settle terms than to start a fight you cannot finish.
entries.14:33: In the same way, anyone who is not willing to give up everything he has cannot be Jesus' disciple. Following Jesus requires putting him above all your possessions and plans.
entries.14:34: Salt is useful, but if it loses its saltiness, it is worthless. Jesus' followers are meant to be distinct and useful, not bland and ineffective.
entries.14:35: Salt that has lost its taste is good for nothing, not even for the soil or the trash heap, so people throw it out. Jesus ends by urging anyone with ears to listen carefully to what he is saying.
entries.15:1: People who were looked down on, like tax collectors and known sinners, came close to listen to Jesus. It shows that Jesus welcomed people others rejected, and that anyone can come to him.
entries.15:2: The religious leaders complained that Jesus was friendly with sinners and even ate with them. Their grumbling sets up the stories Jesus tells next about God's heart for lost people.
entries.15:3: Jesus responded to their complaint by telling them a story. He used everyday pictures to explain what God is really like.
entries.15:4: A shepherd with a hundred sheep would leave the ninety-nine safe and go search for the one that wandered off. God doesn't write off people who stray; he goes after them.
entries.15:5: When the shepherd finds the lost sheep, he carries it home joyfully. God is glad, not annoyed, when a lost person is found.
entries.15:6: The shepherd calls his friends together to celebrate finding his sheep. Heaven's joy over one person coming back is real and shared.
entries.15:7: Jesus says heaven celebrates more over one sinner who turns back to God than over ninety-nine who think they don't need to. No one is too far gone for God to rejoice over.
entries.15:8: A woman who loses one of her ten silver coins lights a lamp and searches carefully until she finds it. God diligently looks for those who are lost, no matter how small they seem.
entries.15:9: When she finds the coin, she invites her friends to celebrate with her. Finding what was lost is worth a party, and God feels the same way.
entries.15:10: Jesus says the angels of God celebrate when one sinner turns from their wrong way. Your turning back to God matters more than you might think.
entries.15:11: Jesus begins a story about a man with two sons. The story shows how God treats people who wander off and those who stay home resentful.
entries.15:12: The younger son demanded his share of the inheritance early, and the father divided his property between them. The father let him go rather than force him to stay.
entries.15:13: The younger son took everything and left for a distant country, where he wasted it all on reckless living. Money and freedom without wisdom lead to ruin.
entries.15:14: When his money ran out, a famine hit that country and he began to go hungry. Bad choices often catch up with us when we least expect it.
entries.15:15: He hired himself out to a local man who sent him into the fields to feed pigs. For a Jewish man, this was about as low as you could go.
entries.15:16: He was so hungry he longed to eat the pigs' food, and nobody gave him anything. Hitting bottom can be what finally makes us stop and think.
entries.15:17: He came to his senses and realized his father's hired servants had plenty to eat while he was starving. Sometimes we need to wake up and see how good we had it.
entries.15:18: He decided to go back to his father and admit he had sinned against God and against him. Real change starts with honest confession.
entries.15:19: He planned to ask his father to take him on as a hired servant, since he felt unworthy to be called a son. He expected punishment, not welcome.
entries.15:20: While he was still a long way off, his father saw him, felt deep pity, ran to him, hugged him, and kissed him. God doesn't wait for you to clean yourself up; he runs to meet you.
entries.15:21: The son confessed that he had sinned and was no longer worthy to be called a son. He said it all, but the father had already forgiven him.
entries.15:22: The father told his servants to bring the best robe, a ring, and shoes for his son. Instead of making him a servant, the father restored him fully as a son.
entries.15:23: The father ordered the fattened calf killed for a celebration feast. God's response to a returning sinner is a party, not a lecture.
entries.15:24: The father said his son had been dead and was now alive, lost and now found, and everyone celebrated. God sees a returning person as coming back to life.
entries.15:25: The older son was out in the field and heard music and dancing as he came near the house. He had no idea what was happening at home.
entries.15:26: He asked a servant what was going on. He was out of the loop on the family's joy.
entries.15:27: The servant told him his brother had returned and their father had killed the fattened calf to celebrate his safe return. The news of grace can be hard to hear for those who feel they've earned their place.
entries.15:28: The older son was angry and refused to go inside, so his father came out and pleaded with him. Resentment can keep us outside the celebration God is throwing.
entries.15:29: He complained that he had served his father for years without ever getting even a young goat to celebrate with his friends. He measured his father's love by what he thought he deserved.
entries.15:30: He resented that his father threw a feast for the son who had wasted the family money. It's easy to be bitter when grace is given to someone we think doesn't deserve it.
entries.15:31: The father told him that he was always with him and everything the father had was already his. The older son already had what he was angry about not getting.
entries.15:32: The father said it was right to celebrate because his brother had been dead and was alive again, lost and was found. God's family celebrates when the lost come home, and he invites the resentful to join in.
entries.16:1: Jesus tells about a rich man who heard that his manager was wasting his money. It reminds us that we are trusted with things that aren't really ours and will have to give an account.
entries.16:2: The rich man calls the manager in and demands a report, then fires him. It means our handling of what we've been given will one day be reviewed, so we should take it seriously.
entries.16:3: The manager panics, knowing he's too weak for hard labor and too proud to beg. It shows how people scramble for security when their position is taken away.
entries.16:4: He hatches a plan to win favor with his master's debtors so they'll take him in after he's fired. It's a picture of someone planning ahead for the future.
entries.16:5: He calls in each person who owes his master money and asks what they owe. He's setting his plan in motion.
entries.16:6: The first debtor owes a large amount of oil, and the manager tells him to quickly change the bill to half. He's cutting the debt to gain the man's gratitude.
entries.16:7: Another debtor owes a large amount of grain, and the manager reduces it too. He's doing the same favor for others to secure his future.
entries.16:8: The master praises the dishonest manager for being clever, and Jesus notes that worldly people are often shrewder about their future than religious people are. It challenges us to be just as thoughtful about our eternal future.
entries.16:9: Jesus tells his followers to use money and resources to make friends who will welcome them into eternity. It means our money should be used for things that last, not just for ourselves.
entries.16:10: Someone who is faithful in small matters will be faithful in big ones, and someone dishonest in small things will be dishonest in big things. It means our everyday small choices reveal and shape our character.
entries.16:11: If you can't be trusted with worldly money, who will trust you with true spiritual riches? It means how we handle money now shows whether we're ready for greater things.
entries.16:12: If you're not faithful with what belongs to someone else, who will give you what's truly your own? It means being trustworthy with what we're entrusted with now matters for what we receive later.
entries.16:13: No one can serve two masters, because you'll end up loving one and hating the other. It means you can't give your ultimate loyalty to both God and money.
entries.16:14: The Pharisees, who loved money, heard all this and mocked Jesus. It shows that people who are attached to wealth often reject teaching that challenges it.
entries.16:15: Jesus tells them they look good to people but God sees their hearts, and what people admire can be disgusting to God. It means God cares about who we really are, not how we appear.
entries.16:16: The Law and the Prophets pointed forward until John, and now the good news of God's kingdom is preached and people are pressing into it. It means a new era has begun with Jesus.
entries.16:17: It's easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for the smallest detail of the Law to fail. It means God's word is completely reliable and won't be set aside.
entries.16:18: Jesus says divorcing your wife to marry another is adultery, and marrying a divorced woman is too. It means God takes marriage promises seriously, even when culture is casual about them.
entries.16:19: Jesus describes a rich man who dressed in luxury and lived in comfort every day. It sets up a story about someone who had everything and noticed nothing.
entries.16:20: A poor man named Lazarus lay at the rich man's gate, covered in sores. It shows the needy person right at the doorstep of someone who could help.
entries.16:21: Lazarus longed for scraps from the rich man's table, and even dogs came and licked his sores. It pictures someone utterly destitute and overlooked.
entries.16:22: The poor man died and angels carried him to Abraham's side, and the rich man also died and was buried. It means death comes to everyone, but their destinies were very different.
entries.16:23: In torment, the rich man looked up and saw Abraham far away with Lazarus at his side. It shows that death reverses the comforts and hardships of this life.
entries.16:24: He begged Abraham to send Lazarus to dip his finger in water and cool his tongue because of the flames. It shows the reality of his suffering and that he still saw Lazarus as someone to serve him.
entries.16:25: Abraham reminds him that he had good things in life while Lazarus had bad things, and now their situations are reversed. It means earthly comfort is not the final word.
entries.16:26: A great gap is fixed between them so no one can cross from either side. It means the separation after death is permanent and can't be undone.
entries.16:27: The rich man asks Abraham to send Lazarus to his father's house. Even in torment, he's thinking about his family.
entries.16:28: He has five brothers and wants Lazarus to warn them so they won't end up in that place of pain. It shows he knows his choices were wrong and doesn't want his family to repeat them.
entries.16:29: Abraham says the brothers already have Moses and the prophets, so they should listen to them. It means God has already given people enough guidance in his word.
entries.16:30: The rich man argues that if someone rose from the dead, his brothers would change their ways. He thinks a miracle would be more convincing than Scripture.
entries.16:31: Abraham says if they won't listen to Moses and the prophets, they won't be convinced even if someone rises from the dead. It means a hard heart won't be changed by miracles if it ignores God's word.
entries.17:1: Jesus says that people will inevitably cause others to stumble, but the person who does it will be held responsible. We should take seriously how our actions affect others' faith.
entries.17:2: Jesus uses a shocking image to show how serious it is to lead a vulnerable person away from faith. It would be better to suffer greatly than to cause a child or new believer to stumble.
entries.17:3: Jesus tells his followers to watch themselves and to confront a fellow believer who sins, but to forgive them if they repent. We should take sin seriously in each other's lives while being ready to forgive.
entries.17:4: Even if someone wrongs you repeatedly in one day, Jesus says to forgive them each time they say they are sorry. Forgiveness should not run out.
entries.17:5: The disciples realize they need more faith to live this way and ask Jesus to increase it. We too can honestly ask God for greater faith.
entries.17:6: Jesus says even a tiny amount of real faith can do what seems impossible, like uprooting a tree. What matters is not how much faith you have but how real and trusting it is.
entries.17:7: Jesus asks a question about a master and his servant to make a point about duty. He is setting up a comparison about how we should see our service to God.
entries.17:8: A master would normally have his servant serve him first before the servant rests or eats. Jesus is showing that service comes before reward.
entries.17:9: The master does not thank the servant for simply doing what he was told. Jesus is pointing out that obedience is expected, not extraordinary.
entries.17:10: Jesus says that when we have done everything God asks, we should not expect special praise. We have simply done our duty as servants.
entries.17:11: Jesus was traveling toward Jerusalem and passed through the region between Samaria and Galilee. This sets the scene for what happens next.
entries.17:12: As Jesus entered a village, ten men with a serious skin disease met him, standing at a distance as the law required. They were isolated and desperate for help.
entries.17:13: The ten men called out loudly to Jesus, asking him to have mercy on them. They knew they needed his help and were not afraid to ask.
entries.17:14: Jesus told them to go show themselves to the priests, and as they went they were healed. Their healing came as they obeyed his word.
entries.17:15: One of the ten saw he was healed and came back, praising God loudly. Gratitude moved him to return and give thanks.
entries.17:16: The one who returned fell at Jesus' feet and thanked him, and he was a Samaritan, an outsider. Jesus notices and honors gratitude from unexpected people.
entries.17:17: Jesus asked where the other nine were, since all ten had been healed. He noticed that only one came back to say thank you.
entries.17:18: Jesus pointed out that only this foreigner came back to give glory to God. It is a gentle rebuke to those who received mercy but did not return thanks.
entries.17:19: Jesus told the man to get up and go, because his faith had made him well. His grateful faith completed what the healing began.
entries.17:20: The Pharisees asked when God's kingdom would come, and Jesus said it would not come in a way you can observe and calculate. God's rule is not something you can pin down by watching for signs.
entries.17:21: People will not be able to point and say the kingdom is here or there, because it is already among you. God's reign is present in your midst, not confined to a location.
entries.17:22: Jesus told his disciples that a time would come when they would long to see one of his days but would not. There would be seasons of longing and waiting.
entries.17:23: People will claim the Messiah is here or there, but Jesus says not to follow them or chase after such claims. Do not be fooled by claims that require you to go searching.
entries.17:24: Just as lightning flashes across the whole sky and cannot be missed, so the Son of Man will be unmistakable when he comes. His return will be obvious to everyone.
entries.17:25: But first Jesus must suffer greatly and be rejected by his generation. Suffering comes before glory in his story.
entries.17:26: The days of the Son of Man will be like the days of Noah, when people carried on with ordinary life. People will be going about their normal routines.
entries.17:27: In Noah's day people were eating, drinking, and marrying right up until the flood came and destroyed them. Ordinary life continued until judgment suddenly arrived.
entries.17:28: Similarly, in Lot's day people were eating, buying, selling, planting, and building. Life went on as usual.
entries.17:29: But on the day Lot left Sodom, fire and destruction fell on everyone there. Judgment came suddenly on that day.
entries.17:30: It will be the same when the Son of Man is revealed. His appearing will bring sudden judgment, just as in those past days.
entries.17:31: On that day, Jesus says, do not go back into the house or field to grab your belongings. Be ready to leave everything behind immediately.
entries.17:32: Jesus tells them to remember Lot's wife, who looked back and was destroyed. Looking back longingly can cost you everything.
entries.17:33: Whoever tries to hold on to his life will lose it, but whoever lets go of it will keep it. Clinging to your life is the way to lose it; releasing it is the way to save it.
entries.17:34: Jesus says that on that night two people will be in the same place, and one will be taken while the other is left. Judgment will divide even those close together.
entries.17:35: Two women will be working side by side at the same task, and one will be taken while the other is left. Being near someone else does not decide your fate.
entries.17:36: This verse says that two men will be in a field, one will be taken and the other left. It reminds the reader that people can be doing the same ordinary things yet end up with very different outcomes.
entries.17:37: The disciples asked where this would happen, and Jesus answered with a picture: where the body is, there the vultures gather. The place of judgment will be obvious, like birds gathering around something dead.
entries.18:1: Jesus told a story to teach that people should keep praying and not give up. It means you should stay persistent in prayer even when nothing seems to happen.
entries.18:2: The story begins with a judge who cared nothing about God or about people. He is an example of someone with no sense of right and wrong.
entries.18:3: A widow kept coming to this judge asking him to give her justice against someone who wronged her. She had no power of her own, so she kept pressing her case.
entries.18:4: For a while the judge refused to help her. Then he thought it over, even though he still didn't care about God or people.
entries.18:5: He decided to give her justice just to get rid of her, because her constant coming was wearing him out. Even a bad judge gave in to persistence.
entries.18:6: Jesus told his listeners to pay attention to what this dishonest judge said. He wanted them to notice the point of the story.
entries.18:7: If even a bad judge helps, God will surely give justice to his people who cry out to him day and night, even if he takes his time. You can trust God to hear your cries.
entries.18:8: Jesus said God will give them justice quickly. Then he asked whether, when he returns, he will find people still trusting him.
entries.18:9: Jesus told this next story to people who were sure they were good and looked down on everyone else. It is a warning about pride in your own goodness.
entries.18:10: Two men went to the Temple to pray: one was a Pharisee, a religious leader, and the other was a tax collector, a job people hated.
entries.18:11: The Pharisee stood and prayed about himself, thanking God he wasn't like other people—crooked, sinful, or like that tax collector. His prayer was really a boast.
entries.18:12: He bragged that he fasted twice a week and gave a tenth of everything he earned. He was listing his religious achievements as if they made him right with God.
entries.18:13: The tax collector stood far off, wouldn't even look up, and beat his chest in sorrow, asking God to have mercy on him as a sinner. He knew he needed help.
entries.18:14: Jesus said the tax collector went home right with God, not the Pharisee. Whoever lifts himself up will be brought down, and whoever humbles himself will be lifted up.
entries.18:15: People brought their babies to Jesus for him to touch, but the disciples scolded them for it. They thought the children were a bother.
entries.18:16: Jesus called the children to him and told the disciples not to stop them, because the kingdom of God belongs to people like them.
entries.18:17: Jesus said that anyone who doesn't receive God's kingdom like a little child will never enter it. It means coming to God with simple trust, not self-importance.
entries.18:18: A rich ruler asked Jesus what he must do to inherit eternal life. He was sincere but thought he could earn it.
entries.18:19: Jesus asked why he called him good, saying only God is truly good. He was pushing the man to think about who he was really talking to.
entries.18:20: Jesus listed some of God's commands: don't cheat on your spouse, don't murder, don't steal, don't lie, and honor your parents. These are the basics of how to treat others.
entries.18:21: The ruler said he had kept all these commands since he was a boy. He believed he had done everything required.
entries.18:22: Jesus told him he still lacked one thing: sell everything, give the money to the poor, and then follow him. He was asking for the man's whole heart.
entries.18:23: The man became very sad at these words, because he was very rich. His wealth was the thing he couldn't let go of.
entries.18:24: Jesus looked at him and said how hard it is for rich people to enter God's kingdom. Money can easily become a rival to God.
entries.18:25: Jesus said it's easier for a camel to go through a needle's eye than for a rich person to enter God's kingdom. It sounds impossible, and that's the point.
entries.18:26: The people listening asked, then who can be saved? If even the rich can't, it seems hopeless for anyone.
entries.18:27: Jesus said what is impossible for people is possible with God. Salvation is God's work, not something we achieve ourselves.
entries.18:28: Peter pointed out that they had left everything to follow Jesus. He was asking, in effect, what will we get?
entries.18:29: Jesus said no one who has left home, family, or loved ones for God's kingdom will lose out. Sacrifice for God is never wasted.
entries.18:30: He promised they will receive far more in this life and eternal life in the world to come. Following Jesus pays back more than it costs.
entries.18:31: Jesus took the twelve aside and told them they were going to Jerusalem, where everything the prophets wrote about him would happen. He was preparing them for what was coming.
entries.18:32: He said he would be handed over to foreigners, mocked, and shamed. He was telling them plainly that suffering was ahead.
entries.18:33: He said he would be beaten, killed, and rise again on the third day. He predicted his death and resurrection in advance.
entries.18:34: The disciples didn't understand any of this; it was hidden from them and they couldn't grasp it. Even clear words can fail to sink in until later.
entries.18:35: As Jesus came near Jericho, a blind man sat by the road begging for money. He was poor and dependent on others' kindness.
entries.18:36: Hearing a crowd passing by, the blind man asked what was going on. He couldn't see, so he had to ask.
entries.18:37: They told him Jesus of Nazareth was passing by. It was news of an opportunity he didn't want to miss.
entries.18:38: The blind man shouted, Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me. He called out to Jesus with faith and desperation.
entries.18:39: People in front told him to be quiet, but he shouted even louder for mercy. He refused to let others silence his cry for help.
entries.18:40: Jesus stopped and ordered the man brought to him, and when he came near, Jesus spoke to him. Jesus noticed the one everyone else tried to hush.
entries.18:41: Jesus stops and asks the blind man what he actually wants, treating him as a person worth listening to. It invites you to bring your real need to God honestly instead of assuming he already knows you don't care.
entries.18:42: Jesus gives the man his sight and credits the man's trust in him as the reason he is healed. It shows that coming to Jesus with confidence, even when things seem hopeless, is what opens the door to his help.
entries.18:43: The man immediately sees, follows Jesus, and praises God, and the crowd joins in praising God too. It means that when God helps you, the natural response is gratitude that also points other people toward him.
entries.19:1: Jesus was passing through the city of Jericho on his journey. This sets the scene for what happens next.
entries.19:2: Zacchaeus was a top tax collector and very rich. Tax collectors were often disliked because they worked for Rome and could take extra money.
entries.19:3: Zacchaeus wanted to see who Jesus was but couldn't because of the crowd, since he was short. Sometimes wanting to see Jesus isn't enough when obstacles get in the way.
entries.19:4: He ran ahead and climbed a tree so he could see Jesus passing by. He was determined enough to look foolish in front of others.
entries.19:5: When Jesus reached the spot, he looked up and called Zacchaeus by name, telling him to come down because he was going to his house. Jesus notices people others overlook and invites himself in.
entries.19:6: Zacchaeus came down right away and welcomed Jesus with joy. Being chosen by Jesus brings real happiness.
entries.19:7: Everyone grumbled that Jesus was going to the home of a sinner. People often resent it when grace is given to those they think don't deserve it.
entries.19:8: Zacchaeus stood up and promised to give half his money to the poor and repay four times over anyone he had cheated. Real change shows itself in how we treat money and people.
entries.19:9: Jesus said salvation had come to that house that day, because Zacchaeus too was a son of Abraham. Jesus declares that this outsider truly belongs to God's family.
entries.19:10: Jesus said his mission was to seek and save those who are lost. He came for people who know they've wandered, not those who think they're fine.
entries.19:11: While people listened, Jesus told another story because he was near Jerusalem and they thought God's kingdom would appear immediately. He wanted to correct their timing.
entries.19:12: He told of a nobleman who went to a distant country to be made king and then return. The kingdom wouldn't come all at once; there would be a waiting period.
entries.19:13: He called ten servants, gave each a sum of money, and told them to do business until he returned. God entrusts us with resources and expects us to use them while we wait.
entries.19:14: His subjects hated him and sent a message saying they wouldn't accept him as ruler. Not everyone welcomes God's authority.
entries.19:15: When he returned as king, he called the servants to account for what they had done with the money. There will be a reckoning for how we used what we were given.
entries.19:16: The first servant reported that his money had earned ten times more. Faithful effort produces results.
entries.19:17: The king praised him as a good servant and gave him authority over ten towns because he was faithful in a small matter. Faithfulness now leads to greater responsibility later.
entries.19:18: The second servant reported that his money had earned five times more. Different results, but still real effort.
entries.19:19: The king gave him authority over five towns. Rewards match faithfulness, not comparison with others.
entries.19:20: Another servant came and handed back the money still wrapped in a cloth, unused. He had done nothing with what he was given.
entries.19:21: He said he was afraid because the master was a hard man, taking what he didn't put down and reaping what he didn't sow. Fear can paralyze us into doing nothing.
entries.19:22: The master judged him by his own words: if he really believed the master was hard, that was all the more reason to act. Our excuses condemn us.
entries.19:23: He asked why the servant hadn't at least put the money in a bank to earn interest. Even minimal effort would have been better than none.
entries.19:24: The master told bystanders to take the money from him and give it to the one who had ten. Unused gifts get taken away.
entries.19:25: They objected that the man already had ten. The master's response seems unfair by human standards.
entries.19:26: Jesus explained that those who have will be given more, but from the one who has nothing, even what he has will be taken. Using what God gives leads to more; neglecting it leads to loss.
entries.19:27: The king ordered his enemies who rejected him to be brought and killed before him. Rejecting God's rule is serious and has consequences.
entries.19:28: After saying this, Jesus went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem. He was moving deliberately toward his final destination.
entries.19:29: Near Bethphage and Bethany by the Mount of Olives, Jesus sent two disciples ahead. He was preparing for his entry into Jerusalem.
entries.19:30: He told them to go into the village ahead, where they would find a young donkey tied up that no one had ever ridden, and to untie it and bring it. Jesus knew in advance what they would find.
entries.19:31: If anyone asked why they were taking it, they should say the Lord needs it. Jesus' authority covers even small details.
entries.19:32: The disciples went and found everything just as Jesus had said. Jesus' words proved true.
entries.19:33: As they were untying the donkey, its owners asked why they were taking it. A natural question when strangers take your property.
entries.19:34: They answered simply that the Lord needed it. That was enough.
entries.19:35: They brought the donkey to Jesus, put their cloaks on it, and Jesus sat on it. He chose to ride a humble animal, not a warhorse.
entries.19:36: As he rode along, people spread their cloaks on the road in front of him. This was a gesture of honor for a king.
entries.19:37: Near the Mount of Olives, the whole crowd of disciples began praising God loudly and joyfully for all the miracles they had seen. Joy overflowed into public praise.
entries.19:38: They shouted blessings on the King who comes in the Lord's name, and peace in heaven and glory on high. They were welcoming Jesus as the promised king.
entries.19:39: Some Pharisees in the crowd told Jesus to silence his disciples. Religious leaders were uncomfortable with the public acclaim.
entries.19:40: Jesus replied that if the disciples were silent, the stones themselves would cry out. His worth is so great that creation itself would praise him if people didn't.
entries.19:41: Jesus came close to Jerusalem and cried out loud over the city. He shows real grief for people who are heading toward trouble, so sorrow for others is not weakness.
entries.19:42: Jesus wished the city could see the path that leads to peace, but it was hidden from them. People can miss what would truly help them, so we should ask God to open our eyes.
entries.19:43: Jesus warned that enemies would build a wall around the city and surround it completely. He was describing a real coming disaster, showing that ignoring God has serious consequences.
entries.19:44: The city and its children would be crushed to the ground, with no stone left standing, because it missed its chance for mercy. Missing God's offer when it comes is a serious loss.
entries.19:45: Jesus entered the temple and drove out the people who were buying and selling there. He cared enough about worship to correct what had been turned into a marketplace.
entries.19:46: Jesus said God's house was meant to be a place of prayer, but they had made it a hideout for thieves. Worship spaces should stay focused on God, not on money and profit.
entries.19:47: Jesus taught in the temple every day, while the religious leaders and rulers looked for a way to kill him. Doing what is right can bring opposition, but Jesus kept teaching anyway.
entries.19:48: They could not act against Jesus because the crowds hung on his words and stayed close to him. People are drawn to honest teaching, and public support can protect someone from harm for a time.
entries.20:1: Jesus was teaching and telling the good news about God in the Temple area. This shows he cared about ordinary people hearing God's message right where they gathered to worship.
entries.20:2: The religious leaders challenged Jesus, demanding to know who gave him the right to teach and act as he did. They were trying to trap him rather than honestly learn from him.
entries.20:3: Jesus answered their challenge with a question of his own. He was turning the tables so they would have to think carefully before answering.
entries.20:4: Jesus asked whether John the Baptist's authority to baptize came from God or merely from people. This put the leaders in a difficult spot about a prophet many people respected.
entries.20:5: The leaders discussed among themselves that if they said John's baptism came from God, Jesus would point out they had not believed John. They were worried about looking foolish.
entries.20:6: They also feared that if they said John's baptism was only human, the crowd might turn on them violently, since the people believed John was a prophet. Their concern was their own safety, not the truth.
entries.20:7: So the leaders claimed they did not know where John's authority came from. They chose to avoid the question rather than admit the truth.
entries.20:8: Jesus then refused to tell them by what authority he acted, since they would not answer his question honestly. He was not going to play their trap game.
entries.20:9: Jesus told the people a story about a man who planted a vineyard, rented it to farmers, and then left for a long time. The story was really about God entrusting his people to their leaders.
entries.20:10: When the owner sent a servant to collect his share of the fruit, the farmers beat him and sent him away empty-handed. This pictures how Israel's leaders had treated God's prophets.
entries.20:11: The owner sent another servant, and the farmers treated him the same way, beating and shaming him. God kept sending messengers, and they kept being rejected.
entries.20:12: A third servant was sent and was wounded and thrown out. The pattern shows how persistently God reached out and how stubbornly the leaders refused to listen.
entries.20:13: The owner decided to send his beloved son, hoping the farmers would respect him. This points to God sending Jesus, his own Son, to his people.
entries.20:14: When the farmers saw the son, they plotted to kill him so the inheritance would become theirs. This foreshadows the religious leaders' plan to kill Jesus.
entries.20:15: They threw the son out of the vineyard and killed him, and Jesus asked what the owner would then do. He was making his listeners think about the coming judgment.
entries.20:16: Jesus said the owner would destroy those farmers and give the vineyard to others, and the people reacted with shock. The warning was that God's blessings would be taken from unfaithful leaders and given to others.
entries.20:17: Jesus pointed to a Scripture about a stone the builders rejected that became the most important stone. He was saying that he, though rejected, was the one God had chosen.
entries.20:18: Anyone who falls on that stone will be broken, and anyone it falls on will be crushed. This means resisting Jesus brings serious consequences.
entries.20:19: The religious leaders wanted to arrest Jesus right then because they knew the story was aimed at them, but they feared the people. They were more afraid of public opinion than of doing what was right.
entries.20:20: They watched Jesus closely and sent spies pretending to be sincere, hoping to catch him saying something they could use against him with the government. They were setting a trap.
entries.20:21: The spies flattered Jesus, saying he taught the truth and showed no favoritism. Their praise was fake, meant to set him up for a trick question.
entries.20:22: They asked Jesus whether it was right to pay taxes to Caesar. This was a trap, since either answer could get him in trouble with the people or the government.
entries.20:23: Jesus saw right through their deceitful plan. He knew exactly what they were trying to do.
entries.20:24: Jesus asked for a coin and pointed out that it had Caesar's image and name on it. The coin itself showed they were already part of the Roman system.
entries.20:25: Jesus said to give Caesar what belongs to Caesar and to God what belongs to God. This means we can fulfill our duties to government while still giving God the ultimate loyalty he deserves.
entries.20:26: The spies could not catch Jesus in anything he said in front of the people, and they were amazed at his answer. His wisdom silenced their trap.
entries.20:27: Some Sadducees, who did not believe in life after death, came to Jesus with a question. They wanted to make the idea of resurrection look foolish.
entries.20:28: They cited Moses' law that if a man died childless, his brother should marry the widow to continue the family line. They were setting up a hypothetical case to stump Jesus.
entries.20:29: They described a situation with seven brothers. This was a made-up scenario designed to create a problem for belief in the resurrection.
entries.20:30: The second brother also married her and died. The story kept building toward their trick question.
entries.20:31: The third brother and then all seven married her and died without having children. The Sadducees were stacking the case to make their point.
entries.20:32: Finally, the woman herself died. The story was complete, and now they would spring their question.
entries.20:33: They asked whose wife she would be in the resurrection, since all seven had married her. They thought this proved resurrection was absurd.
entries.20:34: Jesus explained that people in this present world marry and have spouses. He was distinguishing life now from life after the resurrection.
entries.20:35: Those who are raised to life in the world to come will not marry. Life after the resurrection will be different from life now.
entries.20:36: The raised will no longer die, will be like angels, and will be God's children. This means resurrection life is permanent and free from death.
entries.20:37: Jesus pointed out that even Moses called the Lord the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the burning bush story. Since God is a God of the living, those patriarchs must still be alive to him.
entries.20:38: God is not the God of the dead but of the living, because everyone is alive to him. This means death does not end our relationship with God.
entries.20:39: Some of the scribes responded that Jesus had answered well. Even some of his critics recognized the wisdom in his reply.
entries.20:40: After that, no one dared to ask Jesus any more tricky questions. His wise answers had silenced his opponents.
